title: Physics Foundations: Set 2
description: Twelve independently authored practice questions aligned with the current IB Physics syllabus. New numerical tasks, concise commands and restrained diagrams.

questions.prompt: A launcher sends a small bead horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹. The bead has fallen through a vertical distance of 0.45 m. Air resistance is negligible. What is its horizontal velocity at this point? [1]
questions.hint: Separate the horizontal and vertical motion. With negligible air resistance, identify whether any force changes the horizontal velocity.
notes: For a projectile with negligible air resistance, horizontal acceleration is zero, so the horizontal component of velocity remains equal to its launch value.
Gravity changes the vertical component of velocity. A change in total speed does not imply a change in the horizontal component.

answer.explanation: There is no horizontal resultant force, so the horizontal velocity remains 8.0 m s⁻¹. The drop distance affects vertical motion. D confuses the numerical value of gravitational acceleration with a velocity.

questions.prompt: A test sled starts from rest on a straight horizontal rail. Its acceleration is constant at 0.80 m s⁻² while it travels 3.6 m.
questions.hint: Use the constant-acceleration equations with initial velocity zero.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Select v² = u² + 2as because displacement and acceleration are known but time is not. Set u = 0.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use v = u + at with the speed from part (a), or use s = ½at² directly. The sled does not travel at its final speed throughout.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Consider whether the sled travels at its final speed throughout the interval.

notes: When acceleration is constant, v² = u² + 2as links speeds and displacement without requiring elapsed time. Choose the positive root when the question asks for speed.

For motion from rest with constant acceleration, v = at and s = ½at² describe the same motion. The final speed exceeds the average speed; using time = distance/final speed would underestimate the time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the sled after it has travelled 3.6 m. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken to travel the 3.6 m. [2]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 3.6 m divided by the final speed would not give the time taken. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses v² = u² + 2as with u = 0 and the stated acceleration and displacement.
Obtains 2.4 m s⁻¹.
Uses t = (v − u)/a or t = √(2s/a).
Obtains 3.0 s; accept consistent follow-through from part (a).

parts.label: c
parts.answer: The sled accelerates from rest, so its average speed is below 2.4 m s⁻¹; distance divided by final speed underestimates the time.
parts.working: The speed rises from 0 to 2.4 m s⁻¹, giving average speed 1.2 m s⁻¹ for constant acceleration. Using 2.4 m s⁻¹ as though it were constant gives 1.5 s instead of 3.0 s.

marking_points.text: States that the sled starts from rest and speeds up, so final speed is not sustained.
Explains average speed is lower than final speed, so distance/final speed underestimates elapsed time.

questions.prompt: A person standing on a paddleboard pushes a floating buoy. Which pair of forces is a Newton’s third-law pair? [1]
questions.hint: A third-law pair comes from one interaction: one body exerts a force on the second body, and the second exerts an equal opposite force on the first.
notes: Newton’s third-law forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, and act on different bodies. Identify both bodies in the same interaction.
Forces that balance on one body are not a third-law pair. The equality of an interaction pair does not require either body to be stationary.

options.label: A
options.text: The force of the person on the buoy and the force of the buoy on the person.

options.label: B
options.text: The weight of the person and the upward force of the paddleboard on the person.

options.label: C
options.text: The force of the person on the buoy and the weight of the buoy.

options.label: D
options.text: The upward force of the water on the paddleboard and the weight of the person.

answer.explanation: The person and buoy exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These act on different bodies and form one interaction pair. The other choices combine forces from different interactions or forces acting on the same body.

questions.prompt: Two carts move along a straight horizontal track. A 0.60 kg cart travels to the right at 1.8 m s⁻¹ and strikes a stationary 0.30 kg cart. They attach on impact. The external horizontal impulse during the collision is negligible. Take right as positive.
questions.hint: Find the total momentum before the collision, then equate it to the momentum of the joined carts.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Add m₁u₁ and m₂u₂ using the stated positive direction. The second cart initially has u₂ = 0.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Set the momentum from part (a) equal to (0.60 + 0.30)v. Both carts share one final velocity.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Calculate kinetic energy before and after using each object’s actual speed, then consider the effect of sticking.

notes: Total momentum is the signed sum Σmv. An object at rest contributes zero momentum, but its mass still contributes to the total mass after a sticking collision.

For a system with negligible external impulse, total momentum before and after a collision is equal. In a sticking collision, divide the initial total momentum by the combined mass to obtain the common velocity.
Momentum can remain conserved in a sticking collision even though kinetic energy decreases; compare ½mv² before and after, then account for deformation, heating and sound.

diagram.alt: Two carts before impact: a 0.60 kg cart moving right at 1.8 m s⁻¹ towards a stationary 0.30 kg cart.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total momentum of the two carts before impact. [1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the common velocity immediately after impact. [2]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in total kinetic energy in the collision and explain where that energy goes. [4]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Obtains +1.08 kg m s⁻¹ (or 1.1 kg m s⁻¹ to the right).
Uses conservation of momentum with the combined mass 0.90 kg.
Obtains +1.2 m s⁻¹, or 1.2 m s⁻¹ to the right; accept consistent follow-through from part (a).

parts.label: c
parts.answer: 0.324 J decrease; transferred mainly to deformation, internal energy and sound.
parts.working: Before: ½(0.60)(1.8)² = 0.972 J. After: ½(0.60 + 0.30)(1.2)² = 0.648 J. Decrease = 0.324 J; attachment is inelastic and transforms kinetic energy to internal/deformation/sound stores.

marking_points.text: Obtains initial total kinetic energy 0.972 J; the stationary cart initially has zero kinetic energy.
Obtains final total kinetic energy 0.648 J using the combined mass and common speed; follow-through from (b).
Obtains a decrease of 0.324 J from the two energies; follow-through accepted.
Explains transfer to deformation/internal energy or sound in the inelastic collision.

questions.prompt: A small translating sample increases its speed from u to 1.5u. Its mass is unchanged. By what percentage does the sample’s kinetic energy increase? [1]
questions.hint: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed for fixed mass. Find the ratio of final to initial energy, then subtract the original 100%.
notes: For a translating body of fixed mass, Eₖ = ½mv². Multiplying speed by a factor r multiplies kinetic energy by r².
A final-to-initial ratio and a percentage increase are different. A ratio of R corresponds to an increase of (R − 1) × 100%, rather than R × 100%.

answer.explanation: Efinal/Einitial = (1.5u/u)² = 2.25. The increase is (2.25 − 1) × 100% = 125%. A treats energy as proportional to speed; D gives the final energy as a percentage of initial energy.

questions.prompt: A 0.075 kg foam ball is launched vertically from a cup. It rises 2.4 m above its launch point before stopping momentarily. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.hint: Relate the increase in gravitational potential energy to the initial kinetic energy.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Use ΔEₚ = mgΔh with the stated mass and height.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: At the highest point the ball has no kinetic energy. Set ½mu² equal to the potential-energy increase, then solve for u.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Compare how mass appears in initial kinetic energy and gained gravitational potential energy.

notes: Gravitational potential-energy change near Earth is ΔEₚ = mgΔh. The height difference matters; the arbitrary choice of zero potential energy does not affect the change.

With negligible dissipation, a vertically launched body has ½mu² = mgh at its highest point, where its speed is zero. The mass cancels from u = √(2gh), so the required launch speed depends on the height rather than the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in gravitational potential energy from launch to the highest point. [1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the launch speed of the ball. [2]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the required launch speed would be unchanged for a ball of twice the mass reaching the same height under these assumptions. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Obtains 1.8 J (accept 1.764 J or 1.76 J) using the stated data.
Equates initial kinetic energy to the potential-energy increase.
Obtains 6.9 m s⁻¹ (accept 6.86 m s⁻¹); accept consistent follow-through using part (a).

parts.label: c
parts.answer: Both energy terms are proportional to mass, so mass cancels from ½mu² = mgh; u = √(2gh).
parts.working: At the highest point initial ½mu² has become mgh. Dividing both sides by m gives u² = 2gh, independent of ball mass.

marking_points.text: Relates initial kinetic energy and gained potential energy through ½mu² = mgh.
Cancels mass to conclude u = √(2gh), unchanged for the same height.

questions.prompt: A molten alloy freezes at a constant temperature and transfers 240 J of energy to its surroundings. Its volume change is negligible and it does no mechanical work. Which statement describes the change in its internal energy and the particle model explanation? [1]
questions.hint: Energy leaves the alloy, so first determine the sign of its internal-energy change. Constant temperature fixes average random kinetic energy; identify which other microscopic energy component changes during freezing.
notes: During freezing at constant temperature, the average random kinetic energy of particles remains constant while their interaction potential energy decreases. The corresponding energy is transferred to the surroundings.

Temperature indicates average random kinetic energy, not the whole internal energy. Internal energy can decrease at constant temperature during a phase change; the reverse melting process increases interaction potential energy.

options.label: A
options.text: It decreases by 240 J because the average random kinetic energy of the particles decreases.

options.label: B
options.text: It decreases by 240 J because the interaction potential energy of the particles decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: It is unchanged because the temperature is constant.

options.label: D
options.text: It increases by 240 J because a solid structure forms.

answer.explanation: The alloy transfers 240 J out, so its internal energy decreases by 240 J when no mechanical work is done. Constant temperature means its average random kinetic energy is unchanged. The decrease is in the particles’ interaction potential energy as the alloy freezes.

questions.prompt: Two heated surfaces R and S are modelled as black bodies. Their peak wavelengths are 1.20 μm and 0.80 μm respectively. The schematic spectra are normalized separately so that both peaks have the same plotted height. Use Wien’s constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K.
questions.hint: Use the peak positions to determine temperature; separately normalized peak heights do not compare emitted power.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Rearrange λmaxT = b to T = b/λmax. Convert R’s peak wavelength from μm to metres before substituting.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use the peak wavelengths, then consider what separate normalization does to vertical graph scale.

notes: Wien’s displacement law λmaxT = b uses absolute temperature in kelvin and peak wavelength in compatible units. A shorter peak wavelength corresponds to a hotter black body.
For two black bodies, T₂/T₁ = λmax,1/λmax,2. The constant cancels, so a temperature ratio can be calculated directly from peak wavelengths; do not use Celsius temperatures in that ratio.
Separately normalized spectra show their shapes and peak positions, but equal plotted peak heights do not mean equal emitted intensity or equal total power.

diagram.alt: Separately normalized schematic black-body spectra: dashed curve S peaks at 0.80 μm and solid curve R peaks at 1.20 μm; both plotted peak heights are one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature of surface R. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio TS/TR and explain why the equal plotted peak heights do not imply equal temperatures. [3]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses TR = b/λR with the peak wavelength in metres.
Obtains 2.42 × 10³ K (accept 2.4 × 10³ K).

parts.label: b
parts.answer: TS/TR = 1.5. The curves were normalized separately, so equal plotted peak heights do not represent equal physical emission or equal temperature.
parts.working: By Wien’s law TS/TR = λR/λS = 1.20/0.80 = 1.5. Separately rescaling spectra can make their plotted heights equal without changing the peak wavelengths used to infer temperature.

marking_points.text: Uses inverse peak-wavelength relation TS/TR = λR/λS.
Obtains the dimensionless ratio 1.5.
Explains that separate normalization changes plotted heights; peak positions still show different temperatures.

questions.prompt: A light ray passes from air into a transparent block. The angles shown are measured from the surface: 60° in air and 70° in the block. Take the refractive index of air as 1.00. What is the refractive index of the block? [1]
questions.hint: Snell’s law uses angles to the normal. Convert each stated surface angle using 90° − angle before taking the sine ratio.
notes: In Snell’s law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, each angle is measured from the normal to the boundary. A quoted angle to the surface must first be replaced by its complement.
For entry from air into a higher-index material, the refracted angle to the normal is smaller. Checking this bending direction helps detect an inverted refractive-index ratio.

diagram.alt: A ray crossing a horizontal air–block boundary; the incident and transmitted angles to the surface are labelled 60° and 70°, with a dashed normal.

answer.explanation: The normal angles are 30° in air and 20° in the block. nblock = sin30°/sin20° = 1.46. A reverses this ratio; B and C use the surface angles directly.

questions.prompt: Monochromatic light passes normally through two narrow slits separated by 0.40 mm. A screen is 2.0 m from the slits. The centre of the first bright fringe and the centre of the sixth bright fringe on the same side of the central maximum are 15.0 mm apart. Use the small-angle approximation.
questions.hint: Count the intervals between the two numbered bright fringes, then use Young’s fringe-spacing relation.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: From fringe 1 to fringe 6 there are 6 − 1 equal gaps, not six. Divide the stated total separation by this number.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Rearrange s = λD/d to λ = sd/D. Use the fringe spacing from part (a), converting it and the slit separation to metres before substituting.

notes: In a double-slit pattern, fringe spacing is the centre-to-centre distance between adjacent bright fringes. Fringes numbered 1 and 6 are separated by five intervals, so divide the total separation by five.
Young’s relation s = λD/d links fringe spacing, wavelength, screen distance and slit separation. Convert all lengths to compatible units before rearranging it to λ = sd/D.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the separation of adjacent bright fringes. [1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the light. [3]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and marking points are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Divides 15.0 mm by five and obtains 3.0 mm.
Uses λ = sd/D.
Uses compatible length units for the fringe and slit separations.
Obtains 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (or 600 nm); accept consistent follow-through from part (a).

questions.prompt: Two sensors R and S are attached to a string supporting a standing wave. They are in the two loops immediately on either side of the same node, and neither sensor is at a node. The oscillation period is 0.40 s. R reaches maximum upward displacement at t = 0.60 s. At what time after t = 0.60 s does S next reach maximum upward displacement? [1]
questions.hint: The two loops on either side of a node oscillate in antiphase. The time between opposite displacement maxima is half an oscillation period.
notes: Points within a single standing-wave loop oscillate in phase, while points in neighbouring loops oscillate in antiphase. Their phase difference is π radians, corresponding to half a period.

Maximum upward and maximum downward displacements of a sinusoid are separated by T/2. Translate a relative-phase statement into a time offset using the oscillation period; different amplitudes do not change this phase relationship.

answer.explanation: Sensors in adjacent standing-wave loops oscillate in antiphase. When R is maximally upward, S is maximally downward; S reaches its next upward maximum half a period later. t = 0.60 + 0.40/2 = 0.80 s.

questions.prompt: A stretched string supports a standing wave. A stroboscopic image shows successive nodes A, B and C with AB = BC = 0.18 m. The speed of travelling waves on the string is 54 m s⁻¹.
questions.hint: Successive standing-wave nodes are separated by half a wavelength. Use that wavelength with the wave speed.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: A and B are consecutive nodes, so AB = λ/2. Double the node separation to obtain λ.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use f = v/λ with the wavelength from part (a), rather than with the adjacent-node separation.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: The two points lie in neighbouring loops separated by node B. Compare their displacement directions at the same instant.

notes: Adjacent nodes of a standing wave are separated by λ/2; an adjacent node and antinode are separated by λ/4. Identify which two points a quoted distance connects before calculating wavelength.

The frequency of the standing wave equals the frequency of the travelling waves that form it. Once the wavelength is known, v = fλ gives f = v/λ; node separation cannot be substituted directly for wavelength.
Points within one standing-wave loop move in phase, while points in adjacent loops separated by a node move in antiphase.

diagram.alt: A stroboscopic standing-wave pattern with successive nodes A, B and C; each adjacent-node distance is labelled 0.18 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the travelling waves forming the standing wave. [1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the standing wave. [2]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the oscillations of points halfway between A and B and halfway between B and C compare in phase. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Obtains 0.36 m from twice the adjacent-node separation.
Uses f = v/λ with the inferred wavelength.
Obtains 150 Hz; accept consistent follow-through from part (a).

parts.label: c
parts.answer: The two points oscillate in antiphase, differing by half a cycle, because they lie in adjacent standing-wave loops.
parts.working: All non-node points in one loop move together. Across node B, neighbouring loops move in opposite directions at the same instant, a π rad phase difference.

marking_points.text: Identifies points in adjacent loops separated by node B.
Concludes they oscillate in antiphase or π rad out of phase.
